title: Why One Professor Abandoned the AI Resistance professor-abandoned-ai-resistance
author: Kathryn Palmer
summary: Inside Higher Ed's Kathryn Palmer interviews Scott Latham, a UMass Lowell business professor who in 2024 urged faculty to pump the brakes on AI and has since become an adopter. Latham explains that his early fear that AI would hurt learning and his job gave way as the technology advanced and higher education's predicament worsened. He now coaches students to use AI for experiential projects, such as business proposals for a local Boys and Girls Club. He argues that faculty who refuse to experiment are the ones most at risk, while advising institutions to pick what is distinctive about their community and avoid over-adopting vendor tools. The interview also describes the AI Campus Index, which scores colleges across six areas out of 350 points. It is a useful first-person account of how a prominent skeptic changed his mind, though it also promotes Latham's own project.
points: Latham moved from seeing AI as a CliffsNotes-style threat to learning toward treating it as an opportunity once it matured and campus pressures grew.
Hands-on coaching lets students use AI for real experiential work, as in business proposals written for a local nonprofit.
He predicts that faculty who resist and refuse to experiment, not AI itself, are the ones who will lose their jobs.
His advice to institutions is to use AI to amplify what is unique about a campus and to avoid vendor risk from rapid, broad adoption.
The AI Campus Index scores six areas, with the classroom weighted most heavily, and is meant as a peer benchmark and consumer transparency tool.
quotes: My initial thoughts were that it was going to put me out of a job and that it was not going to be beneficial to the student in the classroom. Those concerns came from within the context of where AI was relative to its capabilities. It was a parrot on steroids.

I saw AI’s capabilities evolve at a pace that I hadn’t even imagined, and I saw the predicament of higher education worsened largely because of the incoming Trump administration. Those two things caused me to shift my perspective on AI from a threat to an opportunity to help higher ed evolve into something that will endure.

I realized that if you coach students to use AI and you are hands-on, you can use AI to do some of the most fantastic experiential learning. For example, this past semester, my students used AI to help write business proposals aimed at growing the Boys and Girls Club of Greater Lowell.
The faculty that it’s going to put out of a job are those that continue to resist and don’t experiment. They have to experiment and shift your perspective because AI is not going away.
Don’t go hog wild and implement AI into every aspect of campus; there’s some risk involved, especially if you bring an AI vendor onto campus and they’re out of business 18 months later.

It looks at six areas: AI in the classroom, AI in campus life, AI in operations, governance and AI, AI and research, and AI workforce readiness. We use Claude and some other proprietary algorithms to [score] each of those six buckets, which add up to 350 possible points.

The real value is that an institution can see how their peer institutions are prioritizing their AI initiatives. It’s also helping institutions look internally and ask: Where are we placing our priorities?
